name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q01 - Prediction of light speed in denser medium

questiontext.text: According to the corpuscular model of light and the wave model of light, what are their respective predictions regarding the speed of light in an optically denser medium compared to a rarer medium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Descartes' corpuscular model of light, developed further by Isaac Newton, refraction towards the normal is explained by assuming an attractive force exerted by the denser medium on light corpuscles. Consequently, this model predicted that light travels faster in an optically denser medium than in a rarer medium.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Wave Theory
In 1678, Christiaan Huygens proposed the wave theory of light. By applying Huygens' principle of secondary wavelets to the refraction of plane wavefronts at an interface, Snell's law gives \(\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{v_1}{v_2}\). Because the ray bends towards the normal in a denser medium (\(r < i\)), the speed in the second medium must satisfy \(v_2 < v_1\). Thus, the wave model predicts a lower speed in the denser medium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the corpuscular model predicts a greater speed in the denser medium, whereas the wave model predicts a lower speed in the denser medium.

answer.text: The corpuscular model predicts a greater speed in the denser medium, whereas the wave model predicts a lower speed in the denser medium.
The corpuscular model predicts a lower speed in the denser medium, whereas the wave model predicts a greater speed in the denser medium.
Both the corpuscular model and the wave model predict a lower speed in the denser medium.
Both the corpuscular model and the wave model predict a greater speed in the denser medium.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q02 - Experimental confirmation of speed in water

questiontext.text: Which historic experiment in 1850 experimentally measured the speed of light in water and decisively verified the prediction of the wave model over the corpuscular model?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The contradiction between the corpuscular model (predicting higher speed in denser media) and the wave model (predicting lower speed in denser media) remained unresolved until a direct laboratory measurement of light speed in a dense medium could be executed.

Step 2: Experimental Evidence
In 1850, the French physicist Léon Foucault carried out an experiment measuring the speed of light in water. His experimental result showed that the speed of light in water is less than the speed of light in air.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This direct experimental determination confirmed the prediction made by Huygens' wave theory and refuted the corpuscular prediction. Thus, the historic experiment was Foucault's measurement of the speed of light in water showing it is less than in air.

answer.text: Foucault's measurement of the speed of light in water showing it is less than in air.
Young's double-slit interference experiment in water.
Descartes' corpuscular scattering experiment in glass.
Hertz's spark-gap radio wave detection in vacuum.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q03 - Rectilinear propagation limit of wave optics

questiontext.text: Under what condition does wave optics reduce to the approximation of geometrical optics, where light can be treated as travelling along straight rays?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Visible light has an extremely small wavelength (typically around \(0.4\,\mu\text{m}\) to \(0.7\,\mu\text{m}\), such as \(0.6\,\mu\text{m}\) for yellow light). In everyday situations, apertures, lenses, and mirrors have dimensions on the order of millimetres or centimetres, which are thousands of times larger than the wavelength.

Step 2: Analysis of the Limit
Because of the smallness of the wavelength in comparison to the dimensions of typical optical devices, wave phenomena like diffraction and interference are confined to narrow regions, and light can be approximated as travelling in straight lines. Geometrical optics is strictly the limiting branch of wave optics in which the finiteness of the wavelength is completely neglected, meaning the limit as wavelength tends to zero (\(\lambda \to 0\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, wave optics reduces to geometrical optics when the wavelength of light is negligibly small compared to the dimensions of apertures and optical components, approaching the limit \(\lambda \to 0\).

answer.text: When the wavelength of light is negligibly small compared to the dimensions of apertures and optical components, approaching the limit \(\lambda \to 0\).
When the wavelength of light is much larger than the dimensions of typical mirrors and lenses.
When light travels exclusively through an optically dense medium having a large refractive index.
When the frequency of the light wave approaches zero while its velocity remains constant.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q04 - Propagation of light waves in vacuum according to Maxwell

questiontext.text: How did Maxwell's electromagnetic theory resolve the historical difficulty of how light waves can propagate through vacuum without any material medium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Early physicists believed that all mechanical waves (like sound or water waves) inherently require a material medium to propagate, leading to the hypothesis of a mechanical ether in vacuum.

Step 2: Maxwell's Electromagnetic Framework
James Clerk Maxwell derived the wave equation from the fundamental laws of electricity and magnetism. According to Maxwell, a time-varying electric field produces a space-and-time-varying magnetic field, and a time-varying magnetic field produces a space-and-time-varying electric field. These mutually regenerating fields propagate through vacuum at the speed of light as transverse electromagnetic waves without requiring any physical substance.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, Maxwell explained propagation through vacuum by establishing that light consists of coupled, mutually regenerating time-varying electric and magnetic fields that propagate as transverse waves.

answer.text: By establishing that light consists of coupled, mutually regenerating time-varying electric and magnetic fields that propagate as transverse waves.
By proposing that vacuum contains an undetectable mechanical ether that undergoes elastic longitudinal oscillations.
By proving that light particles are propelled forward by gravitational radiation through free space.
By demonstrating that light is a longitudinal wave whose propagation does not involve electric or magnetic fields.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q06 - Definition of wavefront and energy propagation direction

Step 2: Direction of Propagation and Wave Rays
By definition, rays of light indicate the path along which wave energy is transferred. In an isotropic medium, the energy of the wave travels in a direction strictly perpendicular (normal) to the wavefront at every point.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Consequently, wave energy propagates perpendicular to the wavefront at every point.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q07 - Shape of wavefronts from point source

questiontext.text: What is the shape of the wavefront emerging from an isolated point source in a uniform isotropic medium near the source, and what shape does a small portion of it approximate at very large distances?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An isolated point source in an isotropic medium emits waves uniformly in all directions at the same speed \(v\). After a time \(t\), the disturbance reaches a distance \(r = vt\) in all directions.

Step 2: Geometric Analysis
The locus of all points at a fixed radial distance \(r\) from the point source having the same phase is a spherical surface, forming a diverging spherical wavefront. As the distance from the source becomes very large, the radius of curvature tends to infinity, and any small portion of this vast sphere can be approximated as a plane wavefront.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the wavefront is spherical near the point source and approximates a plane wavefront at very large distances.

answer.text: Spherical near the point source, approximating a plane wavefront at a very large distance.
Cylindrical near the point source, approximating a spherical wavefront at a very large distance.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q08 - Radius of secondary wavelets in Huygens construction

questiontext.text: In Huygens' geometrical construction, if a wavefront is known at time \(t = 0\), how is the new wavefront at a later time \(t = \tau\) determined in a medium where waves propagate with speed \(v\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Huygens' principle states that each point of a wavefront serves as an independent source of a secondary disturbance, which emits secondary wavelets in all directions at the speed of the wave in that medium.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Construction
To find the position and shape of the wavefront at a later time \(t = \tau\), spheres of radius \(r = v\tau\) are constructed from each point on the initial wavefront at \(t = 0\). The forward common tangent envelope to all these secondary spherical wavelets gives the new forward-moving wavefront at time \(\tau\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the new wavefront is found by constructing secondary wavelets of radius \(v\tau\) from each point of the initial wavefront and drawing their forward common tangent envelope.

answer.text: By constructing secondary wavelets of radius \(v\tau\) from each point of the initial wavefront and drawing their forward common tangent envelope.
By drawing spheres of radius \(v/\tau\) centred at the source and taking their chord plane.
By taking the backward envelope of secondary wavelets of radius \(v\tau/2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q09 - Shortcoming of Huygens model regarding backwave

questiontext.text: What shortcoming existed in Huygens' original geometrical formulation regarding the backward-propagating wave (backwave), and how was it originally treated versus its modern justification?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Conditions and the Geometrical Shortcoming
When spheres of radius \(v\tau\) are drawn around every point on a wavefront \(F_1F_2\), a common tangent envelope exists not only in the forward direction \(G_1G_2\), but also in the backward direction \(D_1D_2\). This would imply the continuous physical generation of a backwave travelling back towards the source, which is not observed in reality.

Step 2: Huygens' Ad-hoc Assumption
To resolve this contradiction, Huygens proposed an ad-hoc assumption: he postulated that the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction.

Step 3: Rigorous Resolution
While this ad-hoc assumption explained the absence of the backwave phenomenologically, it lacked physical justification within his original framework. The absence of the backwave is rigorously justified by modern wave theory (Fresnel-Kirchhoff diffraction theory), which includes an obliquity factor \(\frac{1 + \cos\theta}{2}\) that vanishes at \(\theta = 180^\circ\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The shortcoming was the geometrical prediction of a backwave; Huygens introduced an ad-hoc assumption of zero backward amplitude, which was later rigorously justified by wave theory.

answer.text: The envelope construction geometrically predicted a backwave; Huygens introduced an ad-hoc assumption that wavelet amplitude is zero in the backward direction, which was later rigorously justified by wave theory.
The construction predicted no forward wave; Huygens assumed waves only reflect backward, which was disproved by Maxwell.
The construction predicted infinite wave speed in the backward direction; Huygens assumed speed is zero in reverse.
The construction could only explain reflection; the ad-hoc assumption was that refraction cannot occur in isotropic media.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q10 - Wavefront emerging from convex lens with source at focus

questiontext.text: When a point source of light is placed exactly at the principal focus of a thin converging convex lens, what is the shape of the wavefront emerging from the lens?

Step 2: Optical Delay and Refraction
The rays originating from the focus are refracted by the convex lens such that they emerge parallel to the principal axis. Since wave energy travels perpendicular to the wavefront, rays that are mutually parallel correspond to a surface of constant phase that is planar.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the wavefront emerging from a convex lens when a point source is placed at its focus is a plane wavefront.

answer.text: A plane wavefront.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q11 - Shape of stellar wavefront intercepted on Earth

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q12 - Derivation of Snell law using Huygens principle

questiontext.text: A plane wave \(AB\) in medium 1 (speed \(v_1\)) is incident at angle \(i\) on an interface separating it from medium 2 (speed \(v_2\)). In time \(\tau\), the edge \(B\) advances to \(C\) across distance \(BC = v_1\tau\), while a secondary wavelet expands from \(A\) into medium 2 across distance \(AE = v_2\tau\). Tangent \(CE\) forms the refracted wavefront. What is the ratio \(\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Let \(AC\) be the common hypotenuse of right-angled triangles \(ABC\) and \(AEC\) along the interface.
In right triangle \(ABC\), \(\angle B = 90^\circ\) and the angle of incidence is \(\angle BAC = i\). The opposite side is \(BC = v_1\tau\).
In right triangle \(AEC\), \(\angle E = 90^\circ\) and the angle of refraction is \(\angle ECA = r\). The opposite side is \(AE = v_2\tau\).

Step 2: Trigonometric Relations
From triangle \(ABC\):
\[\sin i = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{v_1\tau}{AC}\]
From triangle \(AEC\):
\[\sin r = \frac{AE}{AC} = \frac{v_2\tau}{AC}\]

Step 3: Calculating the Ratio
Dividing the expression for \(\sin i\) by \(\sin r\):
\[\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{\frac{v_1\tau}{AC}}{\frac{v_2\tau}{AC}} = \frac{v_1}{v_2}\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The ratio \(\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\) is identically equal to \(\frac{v_1}{v_2}\), which confirms Snell's law of refraction.

answer.text: \(\frac{\sqrt{v_1}}{\sqrt{v_2}}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q13 - Wavelength and frequency relation across interface

questiontext.text: A monochromatic light wave of wavelength \(\lambda_1 = 600\,\text{nm}\) travelling in vacuum enters a dielectric medium of refractive index \(n = 1.5\). If the speed of light in vacuum is \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), what are the wavelength \(\lambda_2\) and frequency \(\nu\) of the light inside the medium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Wavelength in vacuum: \(\lambda_1 = 600\,\text{nm} = 600 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Refractive index of medium: \(n = 1.5\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The frequency of light depends solely on the source and remains invariant upon entering another medium:
\[\nu = \frac{c}{\lambda_1}\]
The speed in the medium is \(v_2 = \frac{c}{n}\), and the wavelength in the medium is related by:
\[\lambda_2 = \frac{v_2}{\nu} = \frac{\lambda_1}{n}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Calculate the frequency:
\[\nu = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8}{600 \times 10^{-9}} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8}{6.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 5.0 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\]
Calculate the wavelength in the medium:
\[\lambda_2 = \frac{600\,\text{nm}}{1.5} = 400\,\text{nm}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The speed in the medium is \(v_2 = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8}{1.5} = 2.0 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). Checking the product: \(\nu \times \lambda_2 = (5.0 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}) \times (400 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}) = 2.0 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), which matches \(v_2\).
Thus, the wavelength is \(400\,\text{nm}\) and the frequency is \(5.0 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\).

answer.text: \(\lambda_2 = 400\,\text{nm}\) and \(\nu = 5.0 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q14 - Refraction of sodium light into water

questiontext.text: Monochromatic light of wavelength \(589\,\text{nm}\) is incident from air onto a water surface (refractive index of water \(n = 1.33\)). Taking the speed of light in vacuum as \(3.0 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), what is the speed of the refracted light in water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Speed of light in air/vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Refractive index of water: \(n = 1.33 = \frac{4}{3}\).
Wavelength in air: \(\lambda = 589\,\text{nm}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
The speed of light \(v\) in a medium of refractive index \(n\) is given by:
\[v = \frac{c}{n}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the given values into the formula:
\[v = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{1.33} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8}{\frac{4}{3}} = \frac{9.0}{4} \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1} = 2.2556 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1} \approx 2.26 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Since water is optically denser than air, the speed of light must decrease from \(3.0 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) to approximately \(2.26 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Thus, the speed of refracted light in water is \(2.26 \times 10^8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q15 - Critical angle from wave theory of refraction

questiontext.text: A plane wave travelling in an optically denser medium of refractive index \(n_1 = 1.5\) approaches a boundary with a rarer medium of refractive index \(n_2 = 1.0\). According to Huygens' wave theory of refraction, what is the sine of the critical angle \(\sin i_c\) beyond which no refracted wavefront can be formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Refractive index of first medium: \(n_1 = 1.5 = \frac{3}{2}\).
Refractive index of second medium: \(n_2 = 1.0\).
Wave speeds: \(v_1 = \frac{c}{n_1}\) and \(v_2 = \frac{c}{n_2}\), so \(v_2 > v_1\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From Snell's law derived via Huygens' principle:
\[\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \frac{n_2}{n_1}\]
The critical angle \(i_c\) occurs when the refracted wavefront grazes the interface at an angle of refraction \(r = 90^\circ\), giving \(\sin r = 1\). Therefore:
\[\sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the values into the formula:
\[\sin i_c = \frac{1.0}{1.5} = \frac{1}{\frac{3}{2}} = \frac{2}{3}\]
For any angle of incidence \(i > i_c\), \(\sin r > 1\), which has no real solution; hence no refracted wavefront can form, and total internal reflection occurs.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Since \(n_1 > n_2\), \(\sin i_c = \frac{2}{3} < 1\), which is physically valid.
Thus, the sine of the critical angle is \(\frac{2}{3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q16 - Congruent triangles in Huygens reflection proof

questiontext.text: In Huygens' geometrical proof of the law of reflection for a plane wave incident on a flat reflecting surface \(MN\), why are the angles of incidence \(i\) and reflection \(r\) proved to be equal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A plane wavefront \(AB\) strikes the reflecting boundary \(MN\) at point \(A\). In time \(\tau\), point \(B\) moves to \(C\) across distance \(BC = v\tau\). A secondary spherical wavelet expands from \(A\) with radius \(AE = v\tau\). The tangent plane \(CE\) represents the reflected wavefront.

Step 2: Geometric Analysis
Consider the two triangles \(EAC\) and \(BAC\):
1. Both triangles are right-angled: \(\angle AEC = 90^\circ\) and \(\angle ABC = 90^\circ\).
2. Both share the same hypotenuse, \(AC\).
3. Side \(AE = v\tau\) equals side \(BC = v\tau\).
By the RHS (Right-angle, Hypotenuse, Side) congruence criterion, triangle \(EAC\) is congruent to triangle \(BAC\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Corresponding angles are equal: \(\angle BAC = \angle ECA\), which translates to \(i = r\). Thus, the equality arises because triangles \(EAC\) and \(BAC\) are congruent right-angled triangles with common hypotenuse \(AC\) and equal legs \(AE = BC = v\tau\).

answer.text: Because triangles \(EAC\) and \(BAC\) share a common hypotenuse \(AC\) and have equal sides \(AE = BC = v\tau\), making them congruent right-angled triangles.
Because the incident ray and the reflected ray have different speeds in the reflecting medium.
Because the wave frequency changes upon reflection, forcing \(\sin i = \sin r\).
Because the tangent envelope can only be drawn if the two triangles have zero area.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q17 - Equality of optical transit time through convex lens

questiontext.text: When a convex lens focuses a parallel beam of light to form a real focal point, why do waves travelling along the central axis and rays passing through the outer edge of the lens arrive in identical phase at the focus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A convex lens converts an incident plane wavefront into a spherical wavefront that converges toward its focal point \(F\). All points on a wavefront must oscillate in phase, which means they represent disturbances that departed from the original wavefront at the same time and took equal times to reach the new wavefront.

Step 2: Evaluation of Ray Paths
Consider the central ray along the optical axis versus a marginal ray passing near the edge of the lens:
1. Geometrically, the central ray travels the shortest straight-line distance to the focus.
2. However, the central ray traverses the thickest section of the glass lens, where the speed of light is reduced to \(v = c/n\).
3. The marginal ray travels through much less glass (or almost entirely air), but traverses a longer geometric path.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Balance
The additional optical path length \((n - 1)t\) added by the central thickness \(t\) exactly compensates for the extra geometrical distance traversed in air by the marginal rays. Consequently, the total time \(\tau = \int \frac{ds}{v}\) measured along any ray from the incident wavefront to the focus is identical.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the waves arrive in phase because the total transit time along every ray is identical, the shorter path of the central ray being compensated by its slower speed through the thicker glass.

answer.text: The total transit time along every ray from the object wavefront to the focus is identical because the shorter path of the central ray is compensated by its slower speed through the thicker glass.
Light travels faster in the central region of the glass lens than in the thinner peripheral edges.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q18 - Refraction of plane wavefront by thin prism

questiontext.text: When a plane wavefront is normally incident on a thin glass prism, what causes the emerging wavefront to tilt towards the base of the prism?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a glass prism, the speed of light is reduced to \(v = c/n < c\). The optical delay experienced by any segment of a wavefront is proportional to the thickness of glass it traverses.

Step 2: Analysis of the Wavefront Progression
A prism has a triangular cross-section where the thickness of the glass increases linearly from the apex to the base:
1. The top portion of the incoming plane wavefront passes through the thin apex region with minimal delay.
2. The bottom portion of the wavefront passes through the thickest base section of the glass and is delayed the most.
As a result of this differential time delay, the bottom of the wavefront lags behind the top, producing a tilted plane wavefront emerging tilted towards the base.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The tilt is caused because the lower portion travels through the greatest thickness of glass and experiences the largest time delay.

answer.text: The lower portion of the wavefront travels through the greatest thickness of glass and experiences the largest delay due to the lower speed of light in glass.
The upper portion of the wavefront near the apex travels slower than the lower portion in the base.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q19 - Reflected wavefront from concave mirror

questiontext.text: When a plane wavefront is incident normally on a concave spherical mirror of radius of curvature \(R\), what is the nature and radius of curvature of the reflected wavefront?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A concave mirror has a curved reflecting surface whose centre is receded relative to its edges. Incident parallel rays correspond to an incoming plane wavefront.

Step 2: Huygens Reflection Construction
When the plane wavefront reaches the concave surface:
1. The periphery of the wavefront strikes the mirror first and begins reflecting while the central part is still advancing toward the vertex.
2. Upon complete reflection, the reflected wavefront curves inward, becoming a converging spherical wavefront.
3. This wavefront converges to the principal focal point \(F\) of the mirror, which is located at a distance \(f = R/2\) from the mirror surface.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the reflected wavefront is a spherical wavefront converging to the focal point, with radius of curvature equal to \(R/2\).

answer.text: A spherical wavefront converging to the focal point, with radius of curvature equal to \(R/2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q20 - Invariance of frequency during reflection and refraction

questiontext.text: Why do reflected and refracted light waves both possess exactly the same frequency as the incident light when monochromatic light is incident on an interface separating two media?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Reflection and refraction arise physically through the microscopic interaction of the incident electromagnetic wave with the atomic constituents of the medium.

Step 2: Forced Oscillation Model
The bound electrons and atoms of the matter behave as harmonic oscillators. When an incident light wave with frequency \(\nu\) interacts with them, the periodic electric field exerts a periodic driving force on these charged particles, causing them to execute forced oscillations at the driving frequency \(\nu\). Charged particles undergoing forced oscillations at frequency \(\nu\) radiate electromagnetic waves of precisely the same frequency \(\nu\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Consequently, the frequency of both the reflected and refracted light equals the incident frequency because the constituent atomic oscillators execute forced vibrations at the incident frequency.

answer.text: Atoms in the medium act as oscillators driven into forced oscillations at the exact frequency of the incident wave, re-emitting light at that same frequency.
The speed of light is strictly conserved across all material media regardless of refractive index.
The wavelength of light cannot change when crossing an interface due to the law of conservation of momentum.
The refractive index of any medium is naturally tuned to preserve the photon velocity.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q21 - Energy dependence on amplitude versus propagation speed

questiontext.text: When light travels from an optically rarer medium to an optically denser medium, its speed decreases. Does this reduction in wave speed imply a reduction in the energy carried by the light wave?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In wave theory, the energy density and energy flux carried by a wave are determined by the amplitude of the oscillations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Speed and Energy
The speed of propagation \(v = c/n\) represents how fast wavefronts advance through space, which is determined by the electromagnetic permittivity and permeability of the medium. The energy carried by the wave depends on the square of the electric field amplitude (\(I \propto a^2\)). A change in propagation velocity alone does not imply a loss of energy; the energy of the wave is conserved unless absorption takes place.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the reduction in speed does not imply a reduction in wave energy, because energy depends on the square of the amplitude rather than on the wave speed.

answer.text: No, because the energy carried by a light wave depends on the square of its amplitude, not on its speed of propagation.
Yes, because wave energy is directly proportional to the speed of light.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q22 - Intensity determination in photon picture of light

questiontext.text: In the wave model, the intensity of light is proportional to the square of the wave amplitude. For a given frequency of light, what determines the intensity of light in the photon picture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In quantum theory (the photon picture of light), light consists of localized packets of energy called photons. For light of frequency \(\nu\), each individual photon carries a fixed quantum of energy given by \(E = h\nu\).

Step 2: Definition of Intensity
Intensity is defined as the radiant energy incident per unit area per unit time. Since the energy of each photon \(h\nu\) is constant for a given frequency, the total energy crossing a unit area per unit time is directly proportional to the photon flux—that is, the number of photons crossing that unit area per unit time.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, in the photon picture, intensity for a given frequency is determined by the number of photons crossing a unit area per unit time.

answer.text: The number of photons crossing a unit area per unit time.
The energy of each individual photon, which increases with intensity.
The speed at which photons travel through vacuum.
The rest mass of the photons in the beam.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q23 - Superposition principle for overlapping waves

questiontext.text: According to the superposition principle of waves, what is the resultant displacement produced at a point in a medium when multiple waves overlap simultaneously?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The principle of superposition is the fundamental basis for all wave interference and diffraction phenomena.

Step 2: Statement of Principle
When two or more wave disturbances travel through the same region of a linear medium, each wave propagates independently as if the others were not present. At any given point in space and time, the net displacement of the medium is the vector sum of the separate displacements that each individual wave would produce on its own (\(\vec{y} = \vec{y}_1 + \vec{y}_2 + \dots\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the displacements produced individually by each of the overlapping waves.

answer.text: The vector sum of the displacements produced individually by each of the overlapping waves.
The algebraic product of the amplitudes of the individual waves.
The scalar sum of the intensities of the individual waves.
The difference between the maximum and minimum displacements.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q24 - Definition and criteria of coherent wave sources

questiontext.text: Two vibrating sources of light are classified as coherent if and only if they emit waves:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
To produce a sustained, stable interference pattern with stationary maxima and minima on a screen, the phase relationship between the interfering waves must remain fixed over the observation period.

Step 2: Conditions for Coherence
Two sources are defined as coherent when: 1. They oscillate with the same frequency (or wavelength). 2. The phase difference between the displacements they produce at any arbitrary point does not change with time (\(\frac{d\phi}{dt} = 0\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, two sources are coherent when they have the same frequency and maintain a phase difference that remains constant with time.

answer.text: Having the same frequency and maintaining a phase difference that remains constant with time.
Having identical amplitudes while their phase difference varies continuously and randomly.
That travel in opposite directions at different speeds through the same medium.
Derived from two independent sodium discharge lamps placed closely together.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q25 - Resultant intensity for specific phase difference

questiontext.text: Two identical coherent light sources, each producing an individual intensity \(I_0\) at a point \(P\), interfere with a constant phase difference of \(\phi = \frac{2\pi}{3}\). What is the resultant intensity \(I\) at point \(P\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Intensity of each individual source: \(I_1 = I_2 = I_0\).
Phase difference between the two waves: \(\phi = \frac{2\pi}{3}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For two coherent waves of equal intensity \(I_0\), the resultant intensity \(I\) as a function of phase difference \(\phi\) is given by:
\[I = 4 I_0 \cos^2\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Substitution and Calculation
Substitute \(\phi = \frac{2\pi}{3}\) into the formula:
\[\frac{\phi}{2} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{\pi}{3}\]
Evaluate the trigonometric value:
\[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\]
Square the cosine value:
\[\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\]
Compute the resultant intensity:
\[I = 4 I_0 \times \frac{1}{4} = I_0\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The resultant intensity lies between \(0\) (destructive) and \(4I_0\) (constructive), which is mathematically and physically consistent.
Thus, the resultant intensity at point \(P\) is \(I_0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q26 - Path difference condition for constructive interference

questiontext.text: For two coherent sources vibrating in phase with wavelength \(\lambda\), what is the condition on the path difference \(S_1P \sim S_2P\) to produce constructive interference at point \(P\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Constructive interference occurs when two overlapping coherent waves arrive in phase, so that their crests and troughs coincide, maximizing the resultant displacement and intensity.

Step 2: Relation Between Path and Phase Difference
The phase difference \(\phi\) is related to the path difference \(\Delta x = S_1P \sim S_2P\) by:
\[\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x\]
Constructive interference requires \(\phi = 2n\pi\) (where \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\)).

Step 3: Deriving the Condition
Equating the expressions:
\[\frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x = 2n\pi \implies \Delta x = n\lambda\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, constructive interference occurs when the path difference satisfies \(S_1P \sim S_2P = n\lambda\) (where \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\)).

answer.text: \(S_1P \sim S_2P = n\lambda\), where \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\)
\(S_1P \sim S_2P = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda\), where \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q27 - Condition for complete destructive interference

questiontext.text: When two coherent waves of equal amplitude \(a\) and wavelength \(\lambda\) interfere destructively, what is the path difference between them and the resulting intensity at that location?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Destructive interference takes place when two identical waves meet exactly out of phase (phase difference \(\phi = (2n + 1)\pi\)), so that the crest of one wave cancels the trough of the other.

Step 2: Path Difference Calculation
The path difference corresponding to a phase difference \(\phi = (2n + 1)\pi\) is given by:
\[\Delta x = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi}\phi = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi}(2n + 1)\pi = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda\] where \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\).

Step 3: Resultant Intensity Calculation
The resultant amplitude is \(y = a - a = 0\), and the intensity is:
\[I = 4I_0 \cos^2\left(\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{2}\right) = 0\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, destructive interference requires a path difference of \(\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda\), resulting in zero intensity.

answer.text: Path difference is an odd half-integral multiple of wavelength, \(\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda\), and the resulting intensity is zero.
Path difference is an integral multiple of wavelength, \(n\lambda\), and the resulting intensity is \(2I_0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q28 - Geometric locus of constant path difference fringes

questiontext.text: In a ripple tank or optical setup with two point sources \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), what is the geometric nature of the locus of points in the plane for which the path difference \(|S_1P - S_2P| = n\lambda\) is a constant non-zero value?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The interference pattern in space is determined by the locus of points that share an identical path difference from the two point sources \(S_1\) and \(S_2\).

Step 2: Mathematical Definition of Conic Sections
By definition in geometry, the locus of all points \(P\) in a plane such that the absolute difference of their distances from two fixed points (foci) \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) is a constant (\(|S_1P - S_2P| = \text{constant}\)) is a hyperbola.
For \(n = 0\), the locus is the perpendicular bisector (a straight line degenerate hyperbola). For non-zero values \(n = \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots\), the curves are hyperbolic branches with \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) as foci.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the locus of points of constant path difference in the plane forms a family of hyperbolas with \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) as the focal points.

A set of concentric circles centred midway between \(S_1\) and \(S_2\).
A family of parabolas whose directrix passes through \(S_1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q29 - Incoherent addition from independent sodium lamps

questiontext.text: If two separate, independent sodium discharge lamps illuminate two adjacent pinholes \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), no interference fringes are observed on a distant screen. What is the fundamental physical reason for this observation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Microscopic Origin of Thermal Light
In an ordinary light source like a sodium lamp, light is emitted by millions of individual atoms undergoing independent, uncoordinated quantum transitions. Each atomic emission lasts for approximately \(10^{-10}\,\text{s}\).

Step 2: Analysis of Phase Relationship
Because the two lamps are completely independent, the phase of the light wave emitted from one lamp has no correlated relationship with that of the other. The phase difference \(\phi(t)\) between the two sources changes randomly and abruptly every \(10^{-10}\,\text{s}\).

Step 3: Time-Averaging over Observation Interval
Any standard detector or human eye has a response time (e.g., \(0.1\,\text{s}\)) that is vastly longer than \(10^{-10}\,\text{s}\). The observed intensity is the time average of \(I(t) = 2I_0 + 2I_0 \cos\phi(t)\). Because \(\phi(t)\) varies rapidly and uniformly over \([0, 2\pi]\), the time average \(\langle \cos\phi(t) \rangle = 0\).
Thus, the intensities simply add up as \(I = 2I_0\) at all points, producing uniform illumination without interference fringes.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
No fringes appear because independent atomic sources undergo abrupt phase changes in \(\sim 10^{-10}\,\text{s}\), making the sources incoherent and causing intensities to add directly.

answer.text: Light emitted by independent atomic sources undergoes random, abrupt phase changes on a timescale of \(10^{-10}\,\text{s}\), causing the time-averaged interference term to vanish and intensities to add directly as \(2I_0\).
The light waves from sodium lamps travel at different speeds through air and cannot overlap.
Sodium light consists of longitudinal waves which cannot undergo the principle of superposition.
The frequency of light emitted by sodium atoms is too small to form observable fringes on a screen.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q30 - Intensity at quarter wavelength path difference

questiontext.text: In a wave interference experiment with two coherent sources of equal intensity \(I_0\) emitting waves of wavelength \(\lambda\), what is the resultant intensity at a point where the path difference between the waves is \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Intensity of each individual coherent source: \(I_0\).
Path difference at the given point: \(\Delta x = \frac{\lambda}{4}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The phase difference \(\phi\) corresponding to path difference \(\Delta x\) is:
\[\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x\]
The resultant intensity for two coherent waves of equal intensity is:
\[I = 4 I_0 \cos^2\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Substitution and Calculation
Calculate the phase difference:
\[\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left(\frac{\lambda}{4}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2}\]
Calculate \(\frac{\phi}{2}\):
\[\frac{\phi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{4}\]
Calculate \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) and square it:
\[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \implies \cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\]
Evaluate the resultant intensity:
\[I = 4 I_0 \times \frac{1}{2} = 2 I_0\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
At \(\Delta x = 0\), \(I = 4I_0\); at \(\Delta x = \frac{\lambda}{2}\), \(I = 0\). Halfway at \(\Delta x = \frac{\lambda}{4}\), the intensity is exactly \(2I_0\).
Thus, the resultant intensity is \(2I_0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q31 - Young method of locking phase using primary pinhole

questiontext.text: How did Thomas Young successfully overcome the problem of atomic phase fluctuations and maintain coherence between the two pinholes \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) in his 1801 experiment?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ordinary light sources undergo rapid, uncoordinated phase changes in times of \(10^{-10}\,\text{s}\), making independent sources incoherent.

Step 2: Young's Ingenious Technique
Thomas Young illuminated a single small pinhole \(S\) with a bright source of light. The diverging spherical wavefront spreading out from \(S\) fell symmetrically onto two closely spaced pinholes \(S_1\) and \(S_2\). Because both \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are sampled from the same original wavefront, any sudden, random phase jump occurring at the primary source \(S\) occurs simultaneously and identically at both \(S_1\) and \(S_2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This effectively locks the relative phase difference between \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) at a constant value, creating two coherent secondary sources derived from a single wavefront.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q32 - Dependence of fringe width on slit and screen distance

questiontext.text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the fringe width on the screen is initially \(\beta\). If the distance between the slits and the screen \(D\) is doubled while the slit separation \(d\) is halved, what will be the new fringe width \(\beta'\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial slit separation: \(d\).
Initial screen distance: \(D\).
Initial fringe width: \(\beta\).
New screen distance: \(D' = 2D\).
New slit separation: \(d' = \frac{d}{2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
The fringe width \(\beta\) in Young's double-slit experiment is given by:
\[\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Express the new fringe width \(\beta'\) in terms of the modified parameters:
\[\beta' = \frac{\lambda D'}{d'} = \frac{\lambda (2D)}{\frac{d}{2}} = \frac{2 \lambda D}{\frac{d}{2}} = 4 \left(\frac{\lambda D}{d}\right) = 4\beta\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Fringe width is directly proportional to \(D\) and inversely proportional to \(d\). Doubling \(D\) doubles the width (factor of 2), and halving \(d\) doubles it again (factor of 2), resulting in a net factor of \(2 \times 2 = 4\).
Thus, the new fringe width is \(4\beta\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q33 - Calculation of wavelength from fourth bright fringe

questiontext.text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the slits are separated by \(0.28\,\text{mm}\) and the screen is placed at a distance of \(1.4\,\text{m}\). The distance from the central bright fringe to the fourth bright fringe is measured to be \(1.2\,\text{cm}\). What is the wavelength of the light used?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Slit separation: \(d = 0.28\,\text{mm} = 0.28 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\).
Distance from slits to screen: \(D = 1.4\,\text{m}\).
Order of bright fringe: \(n = 4\).
Position of fourth bright fringe: \(x_4 = 1.2\,\text{cm} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The position of the \(n\)-th bright fringe from the central maximum is given by:
\[x_n = \frac{n\lambda D}{d}\]
Rearranging to solve for wavelength \(\lambda\):
\[\lambda = \frac{x_n d}{n D}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the values into the rearranged formula:
\[\lambda = \frac{(1.2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}) \times (0.28 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m})}{4 \times 1.4\,\text{m}}\]
Evaluate the denominator:
\[4 \times 1.4 = 5.6\,\text{m}\]
Evaluate the numerator:
\[1.2 \times 0.28 \times 10^{-5} = 0.336 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}^2 = 3.36 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\]
Divide numerator by denominator:
\[\lambda = \frac{3.36 \times 10^{-6}}{5.6} = 0.60 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m} = 600 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m} = 600\,\text{nm}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Check fringe width: \(\beta = \frac{x_4}{4} = \frac{1.2\,\text{cm}}{4} = 0.3\,\text{cm} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\).
Then \(\lambda = \frac{\beta d}{D} = \frac{(3 \times 10^{-3}) \times (0.28 \times 10^{-3})}{1.4} = \frac{0.84 \times 10^{-6}}{1.4} = 600\,\text{nm}\), which is consistent.
Thus, the wavelength of the light is \(600\,\text{nm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q34 - Intensity at fractional wavelength path difference

questiontext.text: In a Young's double-slit experiment using monochromatic light of wavelength \(\lambda\), the intensity of light at a point on the screen where the path difference is \(\lambda\) is \(K\) units. What is the intensity of light at a point where the path difference is \(\frac{\lambda}{3}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
At path difference \(\Delta x_1 = \lambda\), the intensity is \(I_1 = K\).
We wish to find the intensity \(I_2\) at path difference \(\Delta x_2 = \frac{\lambda}{3}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Phase difference is related to path difference by:
\[\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x\]
Resultant intensity from two coherent slits is:
\[I = I_{\max} \cos^2\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
For path difference \(\Delta x_1 = \lambda\):
\[\phi_1 = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}(\lambda) = 2\pi\]
\[I_1 = I_{\max} \cos^2\left(\frac{2\pi}{2}\right) = I_{\max} \cos^2(\pi) = I_{\max} (-1)^2 = I_{\max}\]
Thus, the maximum intensity is \(I_{\max} = K\).
Now, for path difference \(\Delta x_2 = \frac{\lambda}{3}\):
\[\phi_2 = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\left(\frac{\lambda}{3}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{3}\]
The half-phase is \(\frac{\phi_2}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}\).
Evaluate the intensity:
\[I_2 = K \cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = K \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{K}{4}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The intensity falls smoothly from \(K\) at \(\Delta x = 0\) to \(0\) at \(\Delta x = \lambda/2\). At \(\lambda/3\), \(\cos(\pi/3) = 0.5\), yielding \(K/4\).
Thus, the intensity is \(\frac{K}{4}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q35 - Minimum path difference for fringe coincidence

questiontext.text: A light beam consisting of two wavelengths, \(\lambda_1 = 650\,\text{nm}\) and \(\lambda_2 = 520\,\text{nm}\), is used in a Young's double-slit experiment. What is the minimum non-zero path difference at which bright fringes due to both wavelengths coincide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
First wavelength: \(\lambda_1 = 650\,\text{nm}\).
Second wavelength: \(\lambda_2 = 520\,\text{nm}\).
Let \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) be the integer fringe orders for the two wavelengths at the coincidence point.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A bright fringe occurs when path difference \(\Delta x = n\lambda\). For bright fringes of both wavelengths to coincide at the same spatial point on the screen, their path difference from the two slits must be identical:
\[\Delta x = n_1 \lambda_1 = n_2 \lambda_2\]
where \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are the smallest positive integers.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Set up the ratio of integers:
\[\frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \frac{520\,\text{nm}}{650\,\text{nm}}\]
Divide both numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor (130):
\[\frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{520 / 130}{650 / 130} = \frac{4}{5}\]
Thus, the smallest integers for the first coincidence are \(n_1 = 4\) and \(n_2 = 5\).
Calculate the path difference:
\[\Delta x = 4 \times 650\,\text{nm} = 2600\,\text{nm}\]
Check with the second wavelength:
\[\Delta x = 5 \times 520\,\text{nm} = 2600\,\text{nm}\] assimilate identical paths.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The 4th bright fringe of \(650\,\text{nm}\) precisely coincides with the 5th bright fringe of \(520\,\text{nm}\) at a path difference of \(2600\,\text{nm}\).
Thus, the least path difference is \(2600\,\text{nm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q36 - Intensity contrast with unequal slit amplitudes

questiontext.text: In a double-slit experiment, two interfering waves have an amplitude ratio of \(\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{3}{1}\). What is the ratio of the maximum intensity to the minimum intensity, \(\frac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}}\), in the resulting interference pattern?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Amplitude ratio: \(\frac{a_1}{a_2} = 3\), so \(a_1 = 3a_2\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The maximum resultant amplitude is obtained when the waves interfere constructively:
\[A_{\max} = a_1 + a_2\]
The minimum resultant amplitude is obtained when the waves interfere destructively:
\[A_{\min} = a_1 - a_2\]
Since intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude:
\[\frac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}} = \frac{(a_1 + a_2)^2}{(a_1 - a_2)^2}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute \(a_1 = 3a_2\):
\[a_1 + a_2 = 3a_2 + a_2 = 4a_2\]
\[a_1 - a_2 = 3a_2 - a_2 = 2a_2\]
Compute the ratio:
\[\frac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}} = \frac{(4a_2)^2}{(2a_2)^2} = \frac{16 a_2^2}{4 a_2^2} = \frac{16}{4} = 4\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The ratio is \(4:1\). Notice that because the slit amplitudes are unequal, the minimum intensity does not drop to zero, reducing fringe contrast.
Thus, the ratio of maximum to minimum intensity is \(4:1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q37 - Effect of liquid immersion on fringe width

questiontext.text: A Young's double-slit experimental setup having a fringe width of \(\beta = 0.40\,\text{mm}\) in air is completely immersed in water without altering any geometric dimensions. What is the new fringe width in water (refractive index of water \(n = \frac{4}{3}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Fringe width in air: \(\beta = 0.40\,\text{mm}\).
Refractive index of water: \(n = \frac{4}{3}\).
Slit separation \(d\) and screen distance \(D\) remain unchanged.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The fringe width in a medium is given by:
\[\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}\]
When immersed in a medium of refractive index \(n\), the frequency \(\nu\) remains constant while the speed of light decreases to \(v = c/n\), reducing the wavelength to:
\[\lambda' = \frac{\lambda}{n}\]
Therefore, the new fringe width is:
\[\beta' = \frac{\lambda' D}{d} = \frac{\lambda D}{n d} = \frac{\beta}{n}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the values into the formula:
\[\beta' = \frac{0.40\,\text{mm}}{\frac{4}{3}} = 0.40 \times \frac{3}{4}\,\text{mm} = 0.30\,\text{mm}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Since water is optically denser than air, the wavelength contracts by a factor of \(4/3\), which must contract the fringe width proportionately.
Thus, the new fringe width in water is \(0.30\,\text{mm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q38 - Distance of third dark fringe from center

questiontext.text: In a Young's double-slit experiment where the fringe width is \(\beta\), what is the linear distance of the third dark fringe from the central bright maximum on the screen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Fringe width: \(\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}\).
Target position: the third dark fringe from the central maximum.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Destructive interference (dark fringes) occurs at positions given by:
\[x_n = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{\lambda D}{d} = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right) \beta\] where \(n\) is a non-negative integer:
- For the first dark fringe (\(n = 0\)): \(x_1 = 0.5\,\beta\).
- For the second dark fringe (\(n = 1\)): \(x_2 = 1.5\,\beta\).
- For the third dark fringe (\(n = 2\)): \(x_3 = 2.5\,\beta\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute \(n = 2\) for the third dark fringe:
\[x_3 = \left(2 + \frac{1}{2}\right)\beta = \frac{5}{2}\beta = 2.5\,\beta\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The third dark fringe is located halfway between the second bright fringe (\(2.0\,\beta\)) and the third bright fringe (\(3.0\,\beta\)), giving \(2.5\,\beta\).
Thus, the distance of the third dark fringe from the central maximum is \(2.5\,\beta\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q39 - Definition and condition for wave diffraction

questiontext.text: What is the phenomenon of diffraction, and under what general condition do diffraction effects become prominent for any type of wave?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Diffraction is a universal wave phenomenon exhibited by all wave motions (sound waves, light waves, water waves, and matter waves).

Step 2: Physical Manifestation and Condition
Diffraction refers to the bending of waves around the sharp edges of an obstacle or slit and their subsequent penetration into the region of geometrical shadow. Because the wavelength of visible light is extremely small (\(\sim 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\)), diffraction effects are negligible in everyday life where objects have dimensions of metres or centimetres. Observable diffraction occurs only when the physical dimensions of the aperture or obstacle are comparable to the wavelength of the wave (\(a \approx \lambda\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, diffraction is the bending of waves around corners into the geometrical shadow, prominent when the obstacle or aperture size is comparable to the wavelength.

answer.text: The bending of waves around corners and spreading into geometrical shadow, occurring prominently when the size of the obstacle or aperture is comparable to the wavelength.
The complete absorption of wave energy at a boundary, occurring when the obstacle is infinitely wide.
The splitting of a wave into its component colors, occurring only when the wavelength tends to zero.
The rectilinear propagation of wave rays, occurring only when the aperture is thousands of times larger than the wavelength.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q40 - Condition for first diffraction minimum at single slit

questiontext.text: When a parallel monochromatic beam of wavelength \(\lambda\) is incident normally on a single slit of width \(a\), why is the first diffraction minimum formed at an angle satisfying \(\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{a}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In single-slit diffraction, the slit of width \(a\) acts as a continuous line of secondary wave sources oscillating in phase.

Step 2: Division of the Slit Aperture
At an angle \(\theta\), the total path difference between the wavelets originating from the two extreme edges of the slit (\(L\) and \(N\)) is \(a \sin\theta \approx a\theta\). When \(a\theta = \lambda\):
1. Imagine dividing the slit \(LN\) into two equal halves, each of width \(a/2\).
2. For every point \(M_1\) in the upper half of the slit, there exists a corresponding point \(M_2\) in the lower half located a distance \(a/2\) directly below it.
3. The path difference between the wavelets from \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) arriving at angle \(\theta\) is \(\frac{a}{2}\theta = \frac{a}{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{a}\right) = \frac{\lambda}{2}\).
4. A path difference of \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\) corresponds to a phase difference of \(\pi\), resulting in complete destructive interference between the pair.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because every point in the top half has a counterpart in the bottom half that cancels it out, the net resultant intensity at \(\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{a}\) is zero, forming the first minimum.

answer.text: The slit can be divided into two equal halves such that wavelets from corresponding points in each half differ in path by \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\) and cancel out pairwise.
All secondary wavelets emerging from the slit arrive at the screen in exactly identical phase.
The slit aperture blocks all light waves whose wavelength is less than \(a\).
The path difference between the two edges of the slit is \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\), extinguishing the beam.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q41 - Angular width of central diffraction maximum

questiontext.text: In the Fraunhofer diffraction pattern produced by a single slit of width \(a\) illuminated by light of wavelength \(\lambda\), what is the total angular width of the central maximum, and how does it compare to the angular width of the secondary maxima?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Slit width: \(a\).
Wavelength of light: \(\lambda\).
Minima occur at angles: \(\theta_n \approx \pm \frac{n\lambda}{a}\) for \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\).

Step 2: Angular Width of Central Maximum
The central maximum is bounded by the first diffraction minimum on either side of the center:
\[\theta_{+1} = +\frac{\lambda}{a} \quad \text{and} \quad \theta_{-1} = -\frac{\lambda}{a}\]
The total angular width of the central maximum is the separation between these two first minima:
\[2\theta_1 = \theta_{+1} - \theta_{-1} = \frac{\lambda}{a} - \left(-\frac{\lambda}{a}\right) = \frac{2\lambda}{a}\]

Step 3: Angular Width of Secondary Maxima
Any secondary maximum lies between two consecutive minima, \(\theta_n = \frac{n\lambda}{a}\) and \(\theta_{n+1} = \frac{(n+1)\lambda}{a}\).
The angular width of any secondary maximum is:
\[\Delta\theta = \theta_{n+1} - \theta_n = \frac{(n+1)\lambda}{a} - \frac{n\lambda}{a} = \frac{\lambda}{a}\]

Step 4: Comparison and Final Answer
Comparing the two widths:
\[\frac{2\theta_1}{\Delta\theta} = \frac{\frac{2\lambda}{a}}{\frac{\lambda}{a}} = 2\]
Thus, the central maximum has an angular width of \(\frac{2\lambda}{a}\), which is twice as wide as any secondary maximum.

answer.text: The angular width of the central maximum is \(\frac{2\lambda}{a}\), which is twice as wide as any of the secondary maxima (\(\frac{\lambda}{a}\)).
The angular width of the central maximum is \(\frac{\lambda}{a}\), which is equal to the width of the secondary maxima.
The angular width of the central maximum is \(\frac{\lambda}{2a}\), which is half the width of the secondary maxima.
The angular width of the central maximum is \(\frac{4\lambda}{a}\), which is four times the width of the secondary maxima.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q42 - Comparison of diffraction band widths for red and blue

questiontext.text: When viewing a narrow slit formed by two razor blades illuminated by a filament bulb through optical filters, how do the diffraction bands observed using a red filter compare with those observed using a blue filter?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The angular position of diffraction minima and the resulting fringe width are directly proportional to the wavelength of the light used: \(\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{a}\).

Step 2: Comparison of Wavelengths
In the visible spectrum, red light has the longest wavelength (\(\lambda_{\text{red}} \approx 700\,\text{nm}\)), whereas blue light has a considerably shorter wavelength (\(\lambda_{\text{blue}} \approx 400\,\text{nm}\)).

Step 3: Application to Fringe Width
Because \(\theta \propto \lambda\), the angular spread of the central and secondary diffraction bands is greater for red light than for blue light: \(\theta_{\text{red}} > \theta_{\text{blue}}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Consequently, the diffraction bands are distinctly wider for red light compared to blue light.

answer.text: The diffraction bands are wider for red light than for blue light because red light has a longer wavelength.
The diffraction bands are wider for blue light than for red light because blue light has a higher frequency.
The diffraction bands have identical widths for both colors because slit width alone determines band spacing.
Diffraction fringes disappear entirely for red light because red light cannot bend around edges.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q43 - Conservation of energy in interference and diffraction

questiontext.text: In both interference and diffraction patterns, regions of zero or low intensity (dark fringes) alternate with regions of high intensity (bright fringes). Does this spatial variation violate the law of conservation of energy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The law of conservation of energy requires that the total energy emitted by light sources must equal the total energy distributed over the detection screen, assuming no absorption.

Step 2: Analysis of Energy Distribution
In interference and diffraction, light waves from different parts of the wavefront or different slits superpose. At destructive interference locations, the wave amplitudes cancel, reducing intensity to zero. However, this energy is not lost; constructive interference increases the resultant amplitude and concentrates the energy into the bright fringes.

Step 3: Quantitative Verification
The spatial average of \(I(\phi) = 4 I_0 \cos^2(\phi/2) = 2 I_0 (1 + \cos\phi)\) over a full cycle of \(\phi\) from \(0\) to \(2\pi\) is \(\langle I \rangle = 2 I_0\), which exactly equals the sum of the individual intensities of the two separate sources (\(I_0 + I_0 = 2I_0\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, energy is strictly conserved through spatial redistribution from dark regions to bright regions without any net creation or destruction.

answer.text: No, because light energy is merely redistributed across space: energy reduced in dark fringes is transferred to bright fringes, leaving total energy conserved.
Yes, because energy is permanently destroyed at dark fringes and created at bright fringes.
Yes, because the average intensity across the pattern is twice the sum of the incident intensities.
No, because the photons at dark fringes are absorbed by the vacuum and re-emitted as infrared heat.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q44 - Transverse nature evidenced exclusively by polarisation

questiontext.text: Which of the following optical phenomena provides unambiguous, definitive proof that light waves are transverse in nature rather than longitudinal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different wave phenomena depend differently on the geometric orientation of wave oscillations relative to the direction of propagation.

Step 2: Comparison Across Wave Types
1. Interference and diffraction occur for all types of waves, including longitudinal waves like sound in air as well as transverse waves.
2. Polarisation refers to confining the vibrations of a wave to a single plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
3. Longitudinal waves oscillate exclusively along the direction of propagation and possess complete cylindrical symmetry about their travel direction; therefore, they cannot be polarised.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The fact that light can be polarised proves conclusively that light waves are transverse electromagnetic waves.

answer.text: Polarisation
Interference
Diffraction
Refraction

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q45 - Intensity transmitted by single polaroid sheet

questiontext.text: When an unpolarised light beam of intensity \(I_0\) from an ordinary lamp passes through a single ideal polaroid sheet, what is the intensity of the transmitted beam, and how does it change when the sheet is rotated about the beam axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nature of Unpolarised Light
Natural unpolarised light consists of rapid, random fluctuations of the electric vector \(\vec{E}\) in all possible directions within the transverse plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

Step 2: Action of a Single Polaroid
An ideal polaroid has a unique pass-axis. For an electric field vector oriented at an angle \(\theta\) to the pass-axis, the transmitted component is \(E \cos\theta\), and the transmitted intensity is \(I(\theta) = I_0 \cos^2\theta\).
Because all orientation angles \(\theta\) are equally probable in unpolarised light, the transmitted intensity is the average over all angles from \(0\) to \(2\pi\):
\[I_{\text{trans}} = I_0 \langle \cos^2\theta \rangle = I_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{I_0}{2}\]

Step 3: Effect of Rotation
Rotating the polaroid sheet changes the orientation of the pass-axis in the plane, but because the incident electric vector is randomly oriented with perfect rotational symmetry in the transverse plane, the average \(\langle \cos^2\theta \rangle\) remains exactly \(1/2\) at every orientation.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the transmitted intensity is \(\frac{I_0}{2}\) and remains completely constant as the polaroid is rotated.

answer.text: The transmitted intensity is \(\frac{I_0}{2}\), and rotating the sheet has no effect on the transmitted intensity.
The transmitted intensity is \(I_0\), and rotating the sheet causes it to drop to zero twice per revolution.
The transmitted intensity is \(\frac{I_0}{4}\), and rotating the sheet causes it to vary sinusoidally.
The transmitted intensity is \(\frac{I_0}{2}\), and rotating the sheet causes the intensity to drop to zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q46 - Malus law calculation for sixty degree orientation

questiontext.text: A linearly polarised light beam of intensity \(I_1\) emerges from a polariser \(P_1\). It is then incident upon an analyzer \(P_2\) whose pass-axis makes an angle of \(60^\circ\) with the pass-axis of \(P_1\). What is the intensity of the light transmitted through \(P_2\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Intensity of polarized light incident on analyzer: \(I_1\).
Angle between pass-axes of polarizer and analyzer: \(\theta = 60^\circ\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Malus' law, when completely plane-polarised light of intensity \(I_1\) passes through an analyzer whose transmission axis is inclined at angle \(\theta\) to the plane of polarisation, the transmitted intensity \(I\) is given by:
\[I = I_1 \cos^2\theta\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Evaluate the cosine of the given angle:
\[\cos(60^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}\]
Square the cosine value:
\[\cos^2(60^\circ) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\]
Substitute into Malus' law:
\[I = I_1 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{I_1}{4}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
At \(\theta = 0^\circ\), \(I = I_1\); at \(\theta = 90^\circ\), \(I = 0\). At \(60^\circ\), \(\cos(60^\circ) = 0.5\), which correctly yields one-quarter of the incident intensity.
Thus, the transmitted intensity is \(\frac{I_1}{4}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q47 - Transmission through rotating polaroid between crossed polaroids

questiontext.text: Two polaroids \(P_1\) and \(P_3\) are set in a crossed configuration so that no light passes through. A third polaroid \(P_2\) is placed between them and rotated. If \(I_0\) is the intensity of polarised light emerging from \(P_1\), at what angle \(\theta\) of the pass-axis of \(P_2\) relative to \(P_1\) is the emerging intensity from \(P_3\) maximum, and what is this maximum intensity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Intensity emerging from \(P_1\): \(I_0\).
\(P_1\) and \(P_3\) are crossed: angle between their pass-axes is \(90^\circ\).
Pass-axis of intermediate polaroid \(P_2\) makes an angle \(\theta\) with \(P_1\).
Angle between pass-axes of \(P_2\) and \(P_3\): \(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Malus' law, light transmitted by \(P_2\) has intensity:
\[I_2 = I_0 \cos^2\theta\]
This light is plane-polarised along the pass-axis of \(P_2\) and is incident upon \(P_3\). The intensity transmitted by \(P_3\) is:
\[I_3 = I_2 \cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = I_0 \cos^2\theta \sin^2\theta\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Algebraic Simplification
Using the double-angle identity \(\sin(2\theta) = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\), so \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta)\):
\[I_3 = I_0 (\cos\theta\sin\theta)^2 = I_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta\right)^2 = \frac{I_0}{4} \sin^2(2\theta)\]
The function \(\sin^2(2\theta)\) reaches its maximum possible value of \(1\) when:
\[2\theta = 90^\circ \implies \theta = 45^\circ \quad \left(\text{or } \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\]
The maximum transmitted intensity is:
\[I_{3,\max} = \frac{I_0}{4} \times 1 = \frac{I_0}{4}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
When \(\theta = 0^\circ\) or \(\theta = 90^\circ\), \(I_3 = 0\), as expected for crossed polaroids without a tilted intermediate sheet.
Thus, maximum transmission occurs at \(\theta = 45^\circ\) with intensity \(\frac{I_0}{4}\).

answer.text: \(\theta = 45^\circ\) with maximum intensity \(\frac{I_0}{4}\)
\(\theta = 90^\circ\) with maximum intensity \(\frac{I_0}{2}\)
\(\theta = 30^\circ\) with maximum intensity \(\frac{I_0}{4}\)
\(\theta = 45^\circ\) with maximum intensity \(\frac{I_0}{2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_MCQ_Q48 - Molecular mechanism of polaroid pass axis

questiontext.text: How do the aligned long-chain polymer molecules in a synthetic polaroid sheet selectively polarise an incident unpolarised light beam?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A polaroid sheet consists of long-chain hydrocarbon molecules (such as polyvinyl alcohol doped with iodine) that are stretched and aligned along a specific microscopic direction.

Step 2: Microscopic Interaction Mechanism
Conduction electrons can move relatively freely along the length of these aligned polymer chains:
1. When an incident light wave has its electric field vector \(\vec{E}\) oriented parallel to the aligned chains, the electric field accelerates these electrons along the chains, doing work and transferring wave energy into thermal dissipation (absorption).
2. When the electric field vector is oriented perpendicular to the aligned chains, electrons cannot move easily across the chains; very little interaction occurs, and this component passes through without significant absorption.

Step 3: Definition of Pass-Axis
Because the perpendicular component is transmitted, the pass-axis (transmission axis) of a polaroid is perpendicular to the alignment direction of its long-chain molecules.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the polaroid absorbs electric field components parallel to the aligned chains and transmits components perpendicular to them.

answer.text: Electrons can freely move along the long polymer chains, absorbing electric field components parallel to the chains, while transmitting electric field components perpendicular to the chains (the pass-axis).
The long polymer chains reflect light waves that have electric field vectors perpendicular to their alignment.
The molecules rotate at the frequency of light, transmitting only components vibrating parallel to the aligned chains.
The polymer chains undergo total internal reflection for all wavelengths except yellow light.
